source.title: Solvable Model for Inheriting the Regularization through Knowledge Distillation

record.tranche_reason: The study tests test-error peaks as training sample size varies in a solvable sparse linear-classifier knowledge-distillation setting, rather than sweeping deep-network size or training epochs.
record.gate_note: The study reports test/generalization-error results versus sample-to-dimension ratio α, including an interpolation-threshold peak and a separability-threshold peak. It also reports that teacher regularization changes the peak behavior. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study analyses replica-theory and simulated test error against samples per dimension α in a knowledge-distillation setting: a logistic-regression teacher and a sparse linear student on Gaussian-mixture data. It finds test-error peaks at the student interpolation threshold (α=η) and at the separability threshold (αS). Raising α toward these thresholds raises test error, which bears on V3 in a new, non-deep setting. Teacher, student and temperature regularization change the peak, which bears on the regularization part of V6. T3 fits better than T2, because this is a new model class and setting rather than a different method on deep networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. Its main conclusion is that KD transfers teacher regularization to the student, and that a Bayes-optimal teacher lets the student approach the optimal bound. On double descent, the authors report a hybrid of regression-type interpolation peaks and classification separability-threshold peaks, appearing with zero direct student regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses replica analysis and finite-size simulations of L2-regularized logistic-regression teachers and sparse linear students on Gaussian-mixture data; it does not reproduce a deep-network size or epoch sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed peak mechanism depends on teacher regularization: weakly regularized teachers yield a student separability-threshold peak, while a finite-regularized teacher yields an interpolation-threshold peak. Over-regularization partially tempers the cusp.

fits_no_version.finding: Which peak appears depends on whether the teacher's outputs are soft or quasi-binary. A regularized teacher gives a regression-like peak at α=η; a weakly regularized teacher gives a classification-type peak at the separability threshold αS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In distillation, where the double-descent peak falls (interpolation versus separability threshold) depends on how soft the teacher's targets are.

record.problems: The model is a simple Gaussian-mixture linear-classifier setting, so the authors caution that results may not generalize to more complex architectures. Replica predictions are non-rigorous. Finite-size simulations use N = 4000 and 10 samples per point; the authors report that optimization sometimes failed to converge within the 2000-epoch cutoff near peaks and separability thresholds.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted for the versions tested. Other reported quantities such as training loss, student norm, and teacher-student MSE are not test-error results for these claim versions.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size in deep networks.
Deep networks and real data are not covered; only the Gaussian-mixture setting with a sparse linear student.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting the peak location across axes.
Label noise or variance is never varied. Multiple peaks within a single curve are not clearly shown.

missing.what: Direct student ridge regularization (dashed curves) removes the αI and αS peaks that appear under pure distillation.
Lower KD mixing parameter χ avoids the interpolation cusp around α=η.
Raising distillation temperature T (1 to 10) mitigates the α=η interpolation peak.
The peak at αI is more pronounced when teacher regularization is near-optimal (λ̃=0.1).

record.verdict_notes: Double descent is a side analysis in a paper about knowledge distillation. The sample-wise peaks are shown in theory curves plus N=4000 simulations. Near the peaks some simulation runs did not converge within 2000 epochs.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over deep-network model size.
The study tests sample-size variation in one Gaussian-mixture, sparse linear-student setting, not other data or model settings.
No capacity sweep across model classes or evidence that risk improves as capacity grows past interpolation.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Teacher-regularization dependence and different peak mechanisms are discussed. Label noise or variance is not varied, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization is not established.
No re-counting of complexity using an effective parameter count or test of whether this turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: η = 0.5 sparse student
rows.size_stated: η = 0.5 fraction of weights trainable; input dimension N = 4000 for numerical experiments
rows.operation_detail: Varied sample-to-input-dimension ratio α in pure distillation; teacher and student used λ̃ = 1e-5 and λ = 1e-5.
rows.measure: Test/generalization error versus α; peak location
rows.value: A generalization-error peak at the student separability threshold αS; αS ≃ 1.75 in the stated setting.
rows.uncertainty: Numerical experiments at N = 4000, 10 samples per point; error bars shown.
rows.locator: Section VI, Figure 5; Appendix C, Figure 11 discussion
rows.note: The authors distinguish this weakly regularized logistic-regression separability peak from the interpolation peak in the regularized-teacher setting.
rows.check: Linked only to V3. This is a single separability-threshold peak in one curve. It shows neither noise-driven peaks, nor multiple peaks in one curve, nor removal by regularization, so the V6 link is dropped. Baseline is the error at lower and higher α on the same curve (Fig. 5 blue curve).

rows.subject: η = 0.5 sparse student
rows.size_stated: η = 0.5 fraction of weights trainable; input dimension N = 4000 for numerical experiments
rows.operation_detail: Varied sample-to-input-dimension ratio α in pure distillation; teacher regularized and student near the unregularized limit.
rows.measure: Test/generalization error versus α; interpolation-threshold peak
rows.value: A sharp generalization-error peak at αI = η = 0.5; below this threshold the student can reproduce the teacher's non-binary outputs, and the authors attribute the peak to overfitting noisy data.
rows.uncertainty: Numerical experiments at N = 4000, 10 samples per point; error bars shown.
rows.locator: Section VI, Figure 5; Appendix C discussion
rows.note: This is the reported case in which increasing sample size reaches an interpolation-threshold test-error peak.
rows.check: Linked only to V3. The authors attribute the peak to overfitting noisy data, but noise is never varied, so the row cannot speak to the noise-driven part of V6. The V6 link is dropped.

rows.subject: η = 0.5 sparse student
rows.operation_detail: Compared the interpolation-peak behavior across teacher regularization levels in pure distillation.
rows.baseline: Teacher λ̃ = 0.1 condition, described as closer to optimal teacher regularization
rows.value: The over-regularized teacher and student have lower maximum norms, partially tempering the generalization cusp.
rows.note: The text reports partial tempering, not elimination, of the cusp.
rows.check: The baseline should also note the text's statement that the peak is more pronounced when teacher regularization is near-optimal (λ̃=0.1). An over-regularized teacher only partially tempers the cusp. This is teacher regularization, not regularization of the student's own loss.
